etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English drippen, druppen, from Old English drypan, from Proto-Germanic *drupjaną (“to fall in drops, drip”), from Proto-Germanic *drupô (“drop”). Akin to West Frisian drippe (“to drip”), Dutch druipen, druppelen (“to drip”), German Low German drüppen (“to drip”), German tropfen, tröpfeln (“to drip”), Norwegian Bokmål dryppe, Norwegian Nynorsk drypa (“to drip”).

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To fall one drop at a time.

quote.citation: c. 1726, Alexander Pope (probable author), The Lamentation of Glumdalclitch
quote.text: Which from the thatch drips fast a shower of rain.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter VIII, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Philander went into the next room […] and came back with a salt mackerel that dripped brine like a rainstorm. Then he put the coffee pot on the stove and rummaged out a loaf of dry bread and some hardtack.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, usually with with) To have a superabundance of valuable things.
(intransitive, of the weather) To rain lightly.
(intransitive) To be wet, to be soaked.
(UK, naval slang, intransitive) To whine or complain consistently; to grumble.

quote.citation: 1995, Sue Innes, Making it work: women, change and challenge in the 1990s, page 21:
quote.text: The Women's Royal Naval Service was integrated with the Royal Navy in November 1993.  […]  Men interviewed by Public Eye (April, 1994) said they should 'stop dripping about it' and that women should learn to 'take it like a man  […]

quote.citation: 2012, I. H. Milburn, Falklands War - Get STUFT:
quote.text: The government had been slowly running down the Royal Navy Organisation to save money on various peoples' budgets, so now we had to sub-contract ships to go to war! So stop dripping and "make it so", all those admirals can't be wrong!
I'm sorry for drippin', but drip is what I do. And one of these days, I'm gon' get dressed and drip all over you.

etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English drippe, from the verb (see above). Compare West Frisian drip (“drip”), Dutch drup (“drip”), Danish dryp (“drip”).

(style, swagger): Compare the verb sense "to have a superabundance of valuable things".

definitions.definition: A falling or letting fall in drops; act of dripping.

quote.citation: 1816, Lord Byron, “Canto III”, in Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage. Canto the Third, London: Printed for John Murray, […], →OCLC, stanza LXXXVI:
quote.text: the light drip of the suspended oar

definitions.definition: (medicine) An apparatus that slowly releases a liquid, especially one that intravenously releases drugs into a patient's bloodstream.
(colloquial, derogatory) A limp, ineffectual, or uninteresting person.

quote.citation: 1994, Richard Curtis, Four Weddings and a Funeral, spoken by Scarlett (Charlotte Coleman):
quote.text: Because most of the blokes I fancy think l'm stupid and pointless—and, so, they just bonk me and then leave me. And the kind of blokes that do fancy me, I think are drips. I can't even be bothered to bonk them. Which does sort of leave me a bit nowhere.

definitions.definition: (architecture) That part of a cornice, sill course, or other horizontal member, which projects beyond the rest, and has a section designed to throw off rainwater.
(slang, uncountable) Style; swagger; fashionable and/or expensive clothing.

quote.citation: 2019, Diego Pedraza, "Dragon Fashion", Deadline (Middle College High School, Stockton, CA), Volume 5, Issue 5, page 4:
quote.text: Hailey decided to show off her drip with a soft, white fluff jacket  […]

quote.citation: 2020 December, “Inside The Winter Chic”, in Brown Sugar Box, page 3:
quote.text: The cold weather can't stop your drip.

quote.citation: 2021 June, “Handpicked Section”, in Syzygy Magazine, page 16:
quote.text: Staying true to their purpose, all this exciting drip will be available at the most pocket-friendly prices.

definitions.definition: (finance) A dividend reinvestment program; a type of financial investing.
